lesson.title: The For Loop: Repeating a Fixed Number of Times
lesson.summary: A for loop repeats a block of code once for each item in a sequence, making it the natural tool whenever you know in advance what you're iterating over.
lesson.body:
A for loop is best understood as a "for each" loop. Rather than counting down some abstract number of repetitions, it walks through a sequence, such as a list, a string, or a range of numbers, one item at a time, and runs its body exactly once per item. This makes the for loop the go-to choice whenever the thing you are repeating over already exists as a collection: a list of students, the characters in a word, the rows of a table read from a file.

The syntax follows a consistent shape: the keyword for, a variable name, the keyword in, an iterable expression, and a colon, followed by an indented block. That variable name is reassigned automatically at the start of each pass, so the body can refer to "the current item" without you writing any counting or indexing logic yourself. Python handles fetching the next element behind the scenes.

Here is a for loop working over a list of strings:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit.upper())
Trace through it carefully. On the first pass, fruit is bound to "apple", and fruit.upper() produces "APPLE", which gets printed. On the second pass, fruit is bound to "banana", printing "BANANA". On the third pass, fruit is bound to "cherry", printing "CHERRY". After that, the list has no items left, so the loop ends on its own, with no condition to check and no counter to update by hand, and execution simply continues with the line after the loop.

That last point is the key difference from a while loop, covered next: a for loop's stopping point is decided entirely by the length of the sequence you hand it. You never have to remember to increment anything or write a comparison that decides when to quit, which removes an entire category of bugs that shows up constantly in other kinds of loops. This makes for loops less error-prone for the extremely common case of "do something to every item in this collection," while a while loop remains the better fit when the number of repetitions depends on a condition that can only be evaluated as the program runs, such as "keep asking until the user types a valid answer," where no fixed list of things to iterate over exists ahead of time at all.

A for loop can also walk directly over the characters of a string, since a string in Python is itself a sequence, just like a list is. Writing for letter in "cat": would bind letter to "c", then "a", then "t", one character per pass, in exactly the same way fruit was bound to each item in the fruits list above, which shows how broadly the same for-loop syntax applies across different kinds of data.

As a general concept, a for loop is one concrete implementation of the "repeat this block" idea introduced with loops as a whole. It answers the "how many times" question by saying: exactly as many times as there are items to iterate over, no more and no less, which is precise, predictable, and usually exactly what you want when working with data you already have sitting in hand.
